subject: Issues with a Hidden Markov Model for Animal Movement

messages.author: 7069744c97b29f52
messages.subject: Issues with a Hidden Markov Model for Animal Movement
parts:
I am attempting to fit a Hidden Markov Model to the GPS locations of a small forest carnivore. I have a version of the model I want to fit running in Stan, but I wanted to give NIMBLE a try because I don't think that Stan will be able to fit the full model I want to fit. Specifically, I am interested in modeling the movement of an animal that switches between resting and active movement. In this model, when the animal is resting the difference between subsequent GPS locations is purely due to observation error, when the animal is not resting the difference between two locations is modeled in terms of the step length and turning angle between two points measured with observation error. 

The attached code summarizes my progress in building up to the model I am attempting to fit. So far I have been successful in:

  1. Including and fitting the von Mises distribution for turning angles
  2. Fitting a simple "single-state" correlated random walk
  3. Including observation error in the correlated random walk
However, I have encountered difficulties in including the state switching in my simulated examples for two cases. My goal eventually is to merge these two cases into the final model.

Case 1:
In the first case, I have attempted to model a standard Hidden Markov Model  for animal movement without observation error. That is, the observed step-length and turning angle depend on the state the animal is in during each timestep and the probability of switching of remaining in the same state in the next timestep is determined by a transition matrix. Rather than marginalizing ("filtering"), I have attempted to model the state as an unobserved discrete variable. I know with this formulation that I can marginalize over the latent states, but hopefully my second case will show why I do not want to do that. When I attempt to fit the code from the first case to simulated data, I get a series of errors from NIMBLE all related to the latent discrete variable z.

Error in envRefInferField(x, what, getClass(class(x)), selfEnv) :
  ‘i’ is not a valid field or method name for reference class “code_MID_77_modelClass_UID_971_UID_972”
Note: cannot calculate logProb for node  z[999] .

The model and simulation code for the first case is in the attached, but for the casual reader here is the code of the model:

switching_CRW <- nimbleCode({
  pi <- 3.141593
  shape[1] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  shape[2] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  rate[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  rate[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  loc[1] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  loc[2] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  kappa[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  kappa[2] ~ T(dnorm(5, sd = 1), 0, )
  remain[1] ~ dbeta(9, 1)
  remain[2] ~ dbeta(1, 9)
  alpha[1, 1] <- remain_1
  alpha[1, 2] <- 1 - remain_1
  alpha[2, 1] <- 1 - remain_2
  alpha[2, 2] <- remain_2
  lambda[1] ~ dunif(0, 1)
  lambda[2] <- 1 - lambda[1]
  phi[1, 1] <- lambda[1]
  phi[1, 2] <- lambda[2]
  
  z[1] ~ dcat(phi[1, 1:2])
  
  steps[1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[1]], rate[z[1]])
  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc[z[1]], kappa[z[1]])
  
  for (i in 3:N) {
    z[i - 1] ~ dcat(alpha[z[i - 2], 1:2])
    steps[i - 1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[i - 1]], rate[z[i - 1]])
    turn_angle[i - 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[i - 2] + loc[z[i - 1]], kappa[z[i - 1]])
  }
})


Case 2:
In the second case, I am attempting to model the switching between a "resting" state and a moving state with observation error. In this case, the discrete state variable is known and included in the model as data. I don't get any errors from this model, rather it seems to fail at the configuration step. When I use nimbleMCMC, I get the following messages, but the MCMC does not run and the mcmc.out object is not saved to the environment:

defining model...
building model...
setting data and initial values...
running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ... 
checking model sizes and dimensions... This model is not fully initialized. This is not an error. To see which variables are not initialized, use model$initializeInfo(). For more information on model initialization, see help(modelInitialization).
checking model calculations...
NAs were detected in model variables: steps, logProb_steps, turn_angle, logProb_turn_angle, lifted_turn_angle_oBt_minus_2_cB_plus_loc_L11, x, y, logProb_xo, logProb_yo.
model building finished.

Again, here is the model code, with the full simulation and R script to run the model in the attached:

switching_CRW_wobserror <- nimbleCode({
  
  pi <- 3.141593
  shape ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  rate ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )

  sigma    ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 0.5), 0, )
  loc   ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  kappa ~ T(dnorm(5, sd = 1), 0, )
  
  steps[1] ~ dgamma(shape, rate)
  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc, kappa)
  
  for(t in 3:N){    
    steps[t - 1] ~ dgamma(shape,  rate)
    turn_angle[t - 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[t - 2] + loc, kappa)
  }
  
  x[1] <- 0
  y[1] <- 0
  for(t in 2:N){
    x[t] <- x[t - 1] + cos(turn_angle[t - 1]) * steps[t - 1] * equals(z[t - 1], 2)
    y[t] <- y[t - 1] + sin(turn_angle[t - 1]) * steps[t - 1] * equals(z[t - 1], 2)
  }

  for (t in 1:N) {
    xo[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], sd = sigma)
    yo[t] ~ dnorm(y[t], sd = sigma)
  }
  
})

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Issues with a Hidden Markov Model for Animal Movement
parts:
Hi Dalton,

Thanks for the questions.

Your first problem seems to reveal a bug in how valid range limits are checked for the dcat.  As a workaround,  please try removing the dcat line for z[i-1] and using the following equivalent code:

  for(i in 1:(N-2)) {
      z[i+1] ~ dcat(alpha[z[i], 1:2])
  }
 
I am less sure about your second problem.  On my system, I get an error from the C stack usage.  While this is an unfortunate boundary to run into, it does reflect that the model as written could be really inefficient.  This happens in state-space models where random effects are propagated through a long series of deterministic state calculations.  For example, in your model, for a sampler to update a value of turn_angle[3] (to pick one), it will need to calculate *all* of x[4]...x[N], y[4]...y[N], and log probabilities of xo[4]...xo[N] and yo[4]...yo[N].  It typically works (much) faster if you can write the x[i] and y[i] as stochastic.  Then to update turn_angle[3], only the log probability of x[4] and y[4] need to be calculated. 

An alternative, if you can't re-write the model that way, would be to use:
x[2:N] <- calculate_xs(x[1:N], turn_angle[1:N], steps[1:N], z[1:N])
and write calculate_xs as a nimbleFunction to calculate the entire series of locations.  In nimble, this will replace 999 scalar nodes with 1 vector node.  If you take that route, you  might as well represent x and y locations jointly in a 2xN matrix and calculate them jointly.

Let us know further questions.

-Perry

Hi Perry,

I was able to get the first case working. Strange that forward looking indices work, but not backward looking. This code works, although I had to turn on WAIC calculation to get to run without errors:

switching_CRW <- nimbleCode({
  pi <- 3.141593
  shape[1] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  shape[2] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  rate[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  rate[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  loc[1] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  loc[2] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  kappa[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  kappa[2] ~ T(dnorm(5, sd = 1), 0, )
  
  remain[1] ~ dbeta(9, 1)

remain[2] ~ dbeta(9, 1)
  
  alpha[1, 1] <- remain[1]
  alpha[1, 2] <- 1 - remain[1]
  alpha[2, 1] <- 1 - remain[2]
  alpha[2, 2] <- remain[2]

lambda[1] ~ dunif(0, 1)
  lambda[2] <- 1 - lambda[1]
z[1] ~ dcat(lambda[1:2])

steps[1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[1]], rate[z[1]])
  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc[z[1]], kappa[z[1]])

for(i in 1:(N-2)) {
    z[i + 1] ~ dcat(alpha[z[i], 1:2])
    steps[i + 1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[i]], rate[z[i]])
    turn_angle[i + 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[i] + loc[z[i]], kappa[z[i]])
  }
})

I'm not sure I following your second suggestion. The problem with writing the x[i] and y[i] as stochastic is that the random variable for the hidden states is on the difference between two locations. This parameterization in terms of step lengths and turning angles is fairly common in the animal movement world and makes it more convenient to look at covariates (for example attraction/repulsion from certain landscape features). But that means that in order to connect the movement process to the locations, one needs to 

I'm looking into an alternative model specification based on a bivariate normal (see Jonsen et al. 2004) that would allow me to more easily write the x[i], y[i] as stochastic when the animal is moving, (i.e. loc[t + 1,1:2] ~ dmnorm(loc[t, 1:2] + ..., sd = Sigma), where loc[t,1]  = x[t]), but this tricky business of including the resting state means that I still need to figure out a way for this to be deterministic when the animal is the resting state. That is, loc[t+1, 1:2] = loc[t, 1:2] when z[t] == 1. 

This is a tricky problem it seems. There are good algorithms for calculating the log-likelihood for hidden markov models without observation error, and good algorithms for observation error in a state space model, but only for a single behavior state. But it seems really tricky to combine the two. Especially with this "resting" state which is basically a zero inflation on the hidden state update.

If I may change the subject briefly back to the Hidden Markov example though. How would I go about encoding the initial state as distributed according to the stationary distribution? That is in my code above and in my simulated example for it, I have that remain[1] = 0.95 and remain[2] = 0.9. Thus alpha is a 2x2 matrix [[0.95, 0.05], [0.1, 0.9]]. The model successfully estimates these parameter correctly now. It also correctly estimates lambda[1] = 0.33..., and lambda[2] = 0.66... but this is a consequence of the Z[1] being distributed according to the stationary distribution which is: 

matrix(c(1,1), nrow = 1) %*% inverse((diag(c(1,1)) - alpha+ matrix(c(1,1,1,1), nrow = 2)))

but if I try to assign that value to lambda, I get an errors about nimMatrix having non-replaceable node values as arguments.

messages.subject: Re: Issues with a Hidden Markov Model for Animal Movement
parts:
Hi Dalton,

About the idea of writing x[i] and y[i] as the stochastic nodes, I think I follow what you are saying.  However I still think there might be a way to do it, either by how the distribution is written or how it is sampled.  In population dynamics state-space models, this makes a big difference.  Let me know if you want to follow up on this.

On to your question about the model declaration for Z[1]: The expression you gave seems to be a 1x2 matrix %*% a 2x2 matrix, which would give a 1x2 matrix, so I don't see how it could be a value for Z[1].  I may not be following what you said correctly.  I am looking at this in terms of code mechanics, not trying to follow your model's logic on this point.  Feel free to attach a reproducible example of this problem.  One issue that comes up in nimble is the need to match types in terms of scalar, 1D, 2D etc.  If you have a matrix expression to create a scalar, it will often actually return a 1x1 matrix or a length-1 vector, so you need to append [1, 1] or [1] to pick out the single element as a scalar, or other indices as needed.  E.g. Hi Perry,

I very much appreciate the assistance. I realize I left off part of sentence in my reply, apologies. What I meant to say is that when using step lengths and turning angles, I don't see an obvious way to not have the latent locations be a deterministic function of the step lengths and turning angles. But I'm sure there is a more efficient way to sample these latent quantities.

I'm certainly interested in learning how write efficient NIMBLE code. Our group (Quantitative Ecology Section of the USGS Western Fisheries Research Center) does a lot of work with JAGS, and I've taken on Stan, but this is my first foray into NIMBLE. I certainly appreciate the ability to implement other probability distributions, and the particle filter and sequential MC is what made me investigate it for this project, but clearly I have alot more learning to do before I attempt to use those samplers. I know the model I want to fit, but I clearly have a lot of questions in terms of implementation.

Your hint on running into a C-stack error, made me think about trying for a smaller version of the model. I was able to get a version of the model working on simulated data by reducing the number of observations. On my first run using this implementation of zero-inflation in step-lengths and turnings angles, I was not able to recover the simulated values. At first I thought that this could be due to inherent identifiability issues in resolving the process error and observation error. So I added in a third variable, "activity" which is assumed to be measured without error, but which is subject to hidden Markov dynamics. This comes directly from the applied problem I am trying to solve: we have a time series of GPS fixes taken every fifteen minutes on a forest carnivore. The GPS fixes are recorded with error, and about 25% of the time the GPS fixes fail altogether because the animal is in deep cover and the GPS is unable to see enough satellites to get a fix. However, for every attempt GPS fix we also have an "activity" measurement, which comes from an accelerometer on the GPS collar and which is a crude summary of how active the animal was in the interval between the current GPS fix and the previous one. 

I was able to get the model including the activity part to run, but I ran into the same issue of not being able to recover the simulated values. However, if I leave out the state-space part of the model (i.e. no observation error) I am able to recover all of the hidden Markov model parameters (step length, turning angle, and transition matrix parameters). Similarly if I leave out the hidden Markov part of the model (i.e. behavioral states are known and treated as data) I am able to recover all of the state-space mode parameters (step length, turning angle, and observation error parameters). Crucially, if I leave out the zero-inflation but otherwise attempt to fit the combined hidden Markov state-space model, I am able to recover the parameters. In this case, the animal switches between a "reduced" movement state (short step lengths, diffuse turning angle) and an "active" movement state (long step lengths, more concentrated turning angles). I actually have this equivalent model working in Stan. My inability to figure out how to implement a version of the model in Stan where one of the movement states is a resting state with step lengths exactly equal to zero is what motivated me to take a look at NIMBLE. But it seems it's a tricky problem here as well. 

My code in exploring NIMBLE for tackling this problem is attached. Part 5 is the example which does not work, all other parts are toy models in which I'm able to recover the parameters. If you have any advice on 1) (most crucially) allowing for a stationary resting state, meaning step-lengths of zero under this parameterization, 2) improving the sampling to avoid crashing or simply having the model fail to run, it would be very much appreciated. I'll continue to noodle around otherwise.




Regarding, my previous question about matrix multiplication in NIMBLE: I'm attempting to fit the initial distribution of the latent state in the hidden Markov model (z[1]) as a categorical variable where the probability of each category is given by the stationary distribution of the Markov process. This is not critical, but it saves me having to estimate a single redundant parameter and helps me understand the quirks of NIMBLE. In my simulated example, I have the transition matrix:

  alpha[1, 1] <- remain[1] #probability of remaining in state 1, simulated as 0.95
  alpha[1, 2] <- 1 - remain[1] #probability of switching to state 2 if in state 1, = 0.05
  alpha[2, 1] <- 1 - remain[2] #probability of switching to state 1 if in state 2, = 0.1
  alpha[2, 2] <- remain[2] #probability of remaining in state 2, = 0.9

With those values, the stationary distribution is a [0.666, 0.333]. Meaning that two-thirds of the time we expect the animal to be in state 1. Because we don't know what state the animal is in prior to the first observation, it makes sense to parameterize the first state according to the stationary distribution. Currently, I'm simply allowing NIMBLE to estimate another parameter for the initial state:

  lambda[1] ~ dunif(0,1)
lambda[2] <- 1 - lambda[1]

z[1] ~ dcat(lambda[1:2]) ## assign behavioral mode for first obs
 
But I know that lamba should really be a function of alpha, hence the matrix math to get there. I was finally able to get a crude calculation to run that looks like this:
  invertible_alpha_trans[1, 1] <- 1 - alpha[1, 1] + 1
  invertible_alpha_trans[1, 2] <- 0 - alpha[1, 2] + 1
  invertible_alpha_trans[2, 1] <- 0 - alpha[2, 1] + 1
  invertible_alpha_trans[2, 2] <- 1 - alpha[2, 2] + 1
  
  inverse_alpha_tran[1:2, 1:2] <- inverse(invertible_alpha_trans[1:2, 1:2])[1:2, 1:2]

  lambda[1] <- inverse_alpha_tran[1, 1] - inverse_alpha_tran[1, 2]
  lambda[2] <- inverse_alpha_tran[2, 1] - inverse_alpha_tran[2, 2]

Aside from being ugly, when I attempt to fit that, the transition parameters appear to stay stuck at their initial values. This is small potatoes in terms of what I want to accomplish, but it strikes me as curious.


Side note: I ran into an error implementing this variable as a beta distribution which appears to be a bug. This works:
  for (t in 1:(N - 1))
    activity[t]   ~ dbeta(a[z[t]], b[z[t]])

but this causes an error, even though it should be equivalent:
  activity[1]   ~ dbeta(a[z[1]], b[z[1]])
  for (t in 1:(N - 2))
    activity[t + 1]   ~ dbeta(a[z[t + 1]], b[z[t + 1]])


Oddly, NIMBLE has no problem with this:
steps[1]   ~ dgamma(shape[z[1]], rate[z[1]])

for (t in 1:(N - 2))
    steps[i + 1]      ~ dgamma(shape[z[i + 1]], rate[z[i + 1]])

I have a version of the model I want to fit running in Stan, but I wanted to give NIMBLE a try because I don't think that Stan will be able to fit the full model I want to fit. Specifically, I am interested in modeling the movement of an animal that switches between resting and active movement. In this model, when the animal is resting the difference between subsequent GPS locations is purely due to observation error, when the animal is not resting the difference between two locations is modeled in terms of the step length and turning angle between two points measured with observation error. 

The attached code summarizes my progress in building up to the model I am attempting to fit. So far I have been successful in:

  1. Including and fitting the von Mises distribution for turning angles
  2. Fitting a simple "single-state" correlated random walk
  3. Including observation error in the correlated random walk
However, I have encountered difficulties in including the state switching in my simulated examples for two cases. My goal eventually is to merge these two cases into the final model.

Case 1:
In the first case, I have attempted to model a standard Hidden Markov Model  for animal movement without observation error. That is, the observed step-length and turning angle depend on the state the animal is in during each timestep and the probability of switching of remaining in the same state in the next timestep is determined by a transition matrix. Rather than marginalizing ("filtering"), I have attempted to model the state as an unobserved discrete variable. I know with this formulation that I can marginalize over the latent states, but hopefully my second case will show why I do not want to do that. When I attempt to fit the code from the first case to simulated data, I get a series of errors from NIMBLE all related to the latent discrete variable z.

Error in envRefInferField(x, what, getClass(class(x)), selfEnv) :
  ‘i’ is not a valid field or method name for reference class “code_MID_77_modelClass_UID_971_UID_972”
Note: cannot calculate logProb for node  z[999] .

The model and simulation code for the first case is in the attached, but for the casual reader here is the code of the model:

switching_CRW <- nimbleCode({
  pi <- 3.141593
  shape[1] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  shape[2] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  rate[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  rate[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  loc[1] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  loc[2] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  kappa[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  kappa[2] ~ T(dnorm(5, sd = 1), 0, )
  remain[1] ~ dbeta(9, 1)
  remain[2] ~ dbeta(1, 9)
  alpha[1, 1] <- remain_1
  alpha[1, 2] <- 1 - remain_1
  alpha[2, 1] <- 1 - remain_2
  alpha[2, 2] <- remain_2
  lambda[1] ~ dunif(0, 1)
  lambda[2] <- 1 - lambda[1]
  phi[1, 1] <- lambda[1]
  phi[1, 2] <- lambda[2]
  
  z[1] ~ dcat(phi[1, 1:2])
  
  steps[1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[1]], rate[z[1]])
  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc[z[1]], kappa[z[1]])
  
  for (i in 3:N) {
    z[i - 1] ~ dcat(alpha[z[i - 2], 1:2])
    steps[i - 1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[i - 1]], rate[z[i - 1]])
    turn_angle[i - 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[i - 2] + loc[z[i - 1]], kappa[z[i - 1]])
  }
})


Case 2:
In the second case, I am attempting to model the switching between a "resting" state and a moving state with observation error. In this case, the discrete state variable is known and included in the model as data. I don't get any errors from this model, rather it seems to fail at the configuration step. When I use nimbleMCMC, I get the following messages, but the MCMC does not run and the mcmc.out object is not saved to the environment:

building model...
setting data and initial values...

checking model sizes and dimensions... This model is not fully initialized. This is not an error. To see which variables are not initialized, use model$initializeInfo(). For more information on model initialization, see help(modelInitialization).
checking model calculations...

model building finished.

Again, here is the model code, with the full simulation and R script to run the model in the attached:

switching_CRW_wobserror <- nimbleCode({
  
  pi <- 3.141593
  shape ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  rate ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )

  sigma    ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 0.5), 0, )
  loc   ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  kappa ~ T(dnorm(5, sd = 1), 0, )
  
  steps[1] ~ dgamma(shape, rate)
  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc, kappa)
  
  for(t in 3:N){    
    steps[t - 1] ~ dgamma(shape,  rate)
    turn_angle[t - 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[t - 2] + loc, kappa)
  }
  
  x[1] <- 0
  y[1] <- 0
  for(t in 2:N){
    x[t] <- x[t - 1] + cos(turn_angle[t - 1]) * steps[t - 1] * equals(z[t - 1], 2)
    y[t] <- y[t - 1] + sin(turn_angle[t - 1]) * steps[t - 1] * equals(z[t - 1], 2)
  }

  for (t in 1:N) {
    xo[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], sd = sigma)
    yo[t] ~ dnorm(y[t], sd = sigma)
  }
  
})
